newsitem.title: USA: Women-run Internet companies still in the minority.
newsitem.headline: Women-run Internet companies still in the minority.

text.p: More women are going online, but starting Internet companies is still a guy thing.

There are some notable exceptions. Kim Polese, co-founder and chief executive at push-technology leader Marimba Inc. (http://www.marimba.com), is often mentioned as an industry rising star, as are venture-capital guru Ann Winblad, co-founder of Hummer Winblad, and Candice Carpenter and Nancy Evans, co-founders of iVillage (http://www.ivillage.com), publisher of the family Web site Parent Soup.

By and large, however, women-owned Internet companies remain in the minority, though it's difficult to determine to what extent. Professional groups such as Women in Technology International (http://www.witi.com) don't track woman-owned Internet businesses, and companies such as IBM (http://www.ibm.com) with marketing teams that sell to women-owned businesses don't separate Internet companies from other enterprises.

But walk through any Internet conference or venture-capital forum and it's not hard to see companies run by men far outnumber women-owned businesses. It's an observation supported by anecdotal evidence from women who've begun Internet ventures, entrepreneurs who believe their time has only now begun.
Just ask Susan Williams DeFife.

DeFife, a former broadcast journalist and one-time press secretary for the governor of Delaware, is founder of Women's Connection Online (http://www.womenconnect.com), a two-year-old Web site for professional women.

DeFife recently attended a venture-capital conference in Atlanta to outline her business plan to would-be investors. Of 60 Internet companies making presentations, two were run by women, DeFife recalls.
"I've been told, your biggest problem is going to be being taken seriously," she said.

Since starting WCO, DeFife has built traffic on the Web site to 400,000 "hits" a month and raised $600,000 in financing. WCO's biggest coup is a partnership with IBM to market Big Blue's GlobalNet Internet access service packaged with WCO editorial material and Web-site building software to women-business owners.

Despite the accomplishments, it wasn't that long ago DeFife was battling age-old prejudices against businesses run by the "weaker" sex. She remembers meeting with a potential banker who quizzed her about the company, only to turn to her partner -- a man -- to talk about finances. Another potential investor wondered aloud whether there were enough "intelligent women in the world" to support a Web site for women managers.
"A woman venture capitalist told my partner she would be more inclined (to finance us) if he were the head of the company because he was more traditionally the kind of CEO they backed," DeFife said.
But the setbacks have been temporary, and support from partners such as IBM encouraging.

"The numbers are growing incredibly fast," said Joan Steltmann, an IBM market executive working with WCO. "Three years ago, 10 percent of Internet users were women. Today it's 42 percent. That's a huge growth rate. The next explosion isn't just women on the net but women using the net for their businesses."

Like DeFife, Julie Jacobs and Pam Shelpuk, co-founders of CyberFlyer Technologies Inc., a Denver start-up selling public Internet kiosks for airports, found it difficult to find investors with enough faith in them to finance their company. Their solution: hire a male-owned consulting firm to help smooth the way. It worked.
"It changed the investment environment for us. Their championing us and believing in us turned the tide," Shelpuk said.

On the other hand, getting suppliers and potential customers to take them seriously was no trouble, said Jacobs and Shelpuk, both airline reservation industry veterans who began the firm that is now CyberFlyer in late 1995.
"I'm more interested in getting their business than who owns it," said David Moser, account executive with BBN Planet, an Internet service provider that links CyberFlyer kiosks to the Internet.

CyberFlyer's biggest contract is with Host Marriott Services to install a minimum of 30 Internet kiosks in seven national airports beginning this summer. When CyberFlyer first bid on the contract, Stan Novack, Host Marriot concept development vice president, didn't know the company's founders were women. Once he found out, he considered it a bonus, considering Host's government-controlled airport customers require suppliers use minority-owned or women-owned businesses as subcontractors, Novack said.

"It wasn't the main reason," he said. "I was impressed when I saw the development they were doing and the services they were offering. And yes, they would bring a different perspective toward business" because they are women.

"The Internet is a great leveler," said Shelpuk. "I don't think we'd be as well positioned in the traditional telecommunications or cable TV business. But because it's the net and it's new and evolving, it's talent that counts. It's not sex. It's the product first."
(Michelle V. Rafter writes about cyberspace and technology from Los Angeles. Reach her at mvrafter(at)deltanet.com. Opinions expressed in this column are her own.)
